newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU summit on track after jobs deal clinched.
newsitem.headline: EU summit on track after jobs deal clinched.

text.p: European Union leaders on Monday swept aside a row over the future of the bloc's plans for monetary union, agreeing a pact to put action for jobs and growth on a par with stringent limits on budget deficits.

The deal, hailed as a breakthrough by France, Britain and the Dutch summit hosts, lifted the clouds which had surrounded the summit and paved the way for agreement on a treaty designed to prepare Europe to welcome new members from the east.

"It is with a great feeling of satisfaction that I can tell you the European Council has reached complete agreement on what our finance ministers decided earlier," Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok told a news conference.
"The light is green for further progress for preparing for EMU," Kok said on the first day of the two-day summit.

France's socialist government, swept to power just two weeks ago on a wave of anger at the austerity measures imposed to ready France for entry into the EU's single currency, said it had started to change the tide of EU policy.

"This is just the start, but we've only been in office for 10 days. We have started to reverse a trend. We have loosened the noose," French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's spokesman, Manuel Valls, told reporters.

Britain's new Labour administration, also claiming credit for reaching a deal which left unchanged the strict economic criteria for entry into the single currency, said Europe would now start to focus on the issues that mattered to citizens.

"The language that we asked for two weeks ago has substantially been accepted...Employment will be and will remain at the top of the agenda," said a senior aide to British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, signalling the end of a heated Franco-German row over how to tackle Europe's high unemployment rate, stressed that the deal involved no extra spending by Europe.
"We can live happily with that, including the resolution on growth and jobs, because it involves no extra resources," Waigel told a news conference.
The deal, which included an agreement to hold a special "jobs summit" later in the year, had little impact in markets.
European stocks, unimpressed by the pact, fell, discouraged by a poor opening on Wall Street, while in currency markets, the dollar was slightly down against the mark.

Dealers said dollar sentiment remained healthy as improved prospects for the launch of the single currency by its scheduled start date in 1999 would result in a "soft" Euro, making the dollar an attractive investment.

But the pact, hammered out first by finance ministers and presented to the leaders for their approval on Monday afternoon, allowed the summit to get back to its scheduled work of dealing with a new treaty paving the way for enlargement.
Leaders were to continue working through a draft treaty on Monday before ordering a new version to be written overnight for agreement on Tuesday.
The treaty, the result of more than 15 months' negotiation, is expected to offer the bloc's citizens a broad range of freedoms and lift internal borders across the continent.

But it is likely to cover up sharp differences between the fervent integrationists who want to move ahead of others if they wish and others who seek opt-outs and protocols to protect vital national positions.
